title: Looking back: the ragas

segments.voice: Yesterday, the close of Sikh thought: God, the self, how to live and the world. Your line was the idea that stayed.

Some songs belong to a time of day. A lullaby at noon sounds wrong. A wedding song at a funeral would be unbearable. The Sikh tradition built that into the scripture itself. Over the year you've met hymns of praise, of longing, of warning, of joy, each under a heading that named its raga before anything else. So as this year of the ways of the Guru begins to close, the looking back starts with the sound under the words: how it was meant to be heard.
screen: `A LULLABY AT NOON SOUNDS WRONG.` → `THE YEAR BEGINS TO CLOSE.` → `HOW IT WAS MEANT TO BE HEARD.`

segments.voice: First, the headings. You met this a week ago: after the opening prayers, the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raga. The hymns sat under raga names, like a door you walk through before you hear a word. Second, a raga is a mood. Musicians in the tradition speak of each one having its own color and its own hour. In Sikh practice, Asa di Var is sung in the early morning. Tradition links Basant with spring and Malar with the rains. The Word doesn't change, but it arrives dressed for the moment. Third, the moods are honest. The Granth doesn't stay cheerful. In Raag Tukhari, Guru Nanak's song of the months walks through the year as a bride longing for her beloved: the heat, the rain, the cold, each month its own ache, until union comes. Longing gets its own music. So does warning, so does celebration. Nobody is asked to fake a mood they're not in. Fourth, one Word, many moods. The same Name is sung in grief and in joy, at dawn and at night, in spring and in the rains. There's a raga for whatever state you walk in with, which means no mood has to be fixed before coming near the Word. You bring the mood. The music meets it.
screen: `HYMNS UNDER A RAGA'S NAME.` · `A RAGA IS A MOOD AND AN HOUR.` · `TUKHARI: THE SONG OF THE MONTHS.` · `ONE WORD, MANY MOODS.` · then, large: `MANY MOODS.`

segments.voice: Name your mood right now, honestly, in one word, tired, hopeful, restless, sad, light, without correcting it. Then ask which hour and season it belongs to, dawn or deep night, spring or the cold, and let them settle around you, the way a raga heading sits over a hymn. Breathe inside it, and notice whether the mood shifts or just feels accompanied.
Looking back. At the year's close, the ragas: hymns under a mood's name, one Word sung for every state you're in. Today's word.
Your line: many moods. Dawn or deep night, there's music for it. Day fourteen hundred twenty.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras, ragis (kirtan musicians) sing hymns in the raga named at their head, and Sikh practice sets particular hymns, such as Asa di Var in the morning, for particular times.

chat.says: Why is the Granth arranged by raga? Isn't it the words that matter?
options: Each raga gives the words a mood, so one Word meets you in every state.
The ragas are only labels, to show which Guru wrote each of the hymns.
Each raga is for one festival, and its hymns are sung only on that day.
